```{r}
#| label: setup

library(nflreadr)
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

# Same data-building code as Milestones 2 and 3
injuries <- load_injuries(2016:2025)

weekly_injuries <- injuries |>
  filter(week %in% 1:17) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(report_primary_injury),
    report_primary_injury != "Not injury related - resting player"
  ) |>
  group_by(season, week) |>
  summarise(injury_reports = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(season, week) |>
  mutate(time = (season - 2016) * 17 + week) |>
  as_tsibble(index = time)

train <- weekly_injuries |> filter(time <= 153)

# Larger text for slides
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))

# x-axis breaks at Week 1 of each season (2016-2026)
season_breaks <- (0:10) * 17 + 1
season_labels <- 2016:2026
```

## The question

- Has the number of NFL injury reports per week changed since 2016?
- How many injury reports should we expect each week next season?
- Who cares: the NFL and the NFL Players Association (player safety),
  and team medical staffs planning for a 17-week season.
- Forecast horizon: 17 weeks, one full regular season.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. Motivate the question and the decision-maker. About 1 minute.
:::

## The data

```{r}
#| label: plot-series

weekly_injuries |>
  autoplot(injury_reports) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = season_breaks[1:10],
    labels = season_labels[1:10]
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly NFL injury reports, Weeks 1–17, 2016–2025",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Injury reports"
  )
```

- Source: nflverse injury reports (`nflreadr`), 170 weeks; resting-player reports excluded.
- No long-run trend after 2016; 2016 is unusually high.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. Explain what one observation is (a count of injury-report records in one
week), and that seasons are joined end to end with no off-season gap.
:::

## A strong week-of-season pattern

```{r}
#| label: plot-season

weekly_injuries |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = injury_reports, group = season, color = factor(season))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:17) +
  labs(
    title = "Each season, Week 1 is far lower than the rest",
    x = "Week of season",
    y = "Injury reports",
    color = "Season"
  )
```

- Week 1 is low every season; counts plateau from about Week 3 on.
- Seasonal strength 0.68: the season shape explains much of the variation.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. This is why every model uses a 17-week seasonal period. Mention briefly
that gg_season() does not work on our week index, so we built this plot by hand.
:::

## Models and how we compared them

- Benchmarks: mean, naive, seasonal naive, random walk with drift
- Exponential smoothing: ETS(M,Ad,A)
- ARIMA(1,1,1)(2,1,0)[17]
- Regression: trend plus week-of-season dummies
- Test set: the 2025 season (train on 2016–2024)
- Time series cross-validation: 5 folds, each forecasting a full season
- Measures: RMSE, MAE, MASE and CRPS

Our prediction: ETS or regression would win, because they average the season shape over many years.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. Keep this quick; the audience knows the methods. Emphasize that the
test set is exactly one forecast horizon and that CV gives five more checks.
:::

## Results: the simplest seasonal model wins

```{r}
#| label: plot-accuracy

models <- function(data) {
  data |>
    model(
      Mean = MEAN(injury_reports),
      Naive = NAIVE(injury_reports),
      `Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(injury_reports ~ lag(17)),
      Drift = RW(injury_reports ~ drift()),
      ETS = ETS(injury_reports ~ season(period = 17)),
      ARIMA = ARIMA(injury_reports ~ PDQ(period = 17)),
      Regression = TSLM(injury_reports ~ trend() + season(period = 17))
    )
}

acc_test <- train |>
  models() |>
  forecast(h = 17) |>
  accuracy(weekly_injuries, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE), .period = 17) |>
  mutate(evaluation = "2025 test season")

acc_cv <- weekly_injuries |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 85, .step = 17) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id)) |>
  models() |>
  forecast(h = 17) |>
  accuracy(weekly_injuries, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE), .period = 17) |>
  mutate(evaluation = "Cross-validation (5 seasons)")

bind_rows(acc_test, acc_cv) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = RMSE, y = reorder(.model, -RMSE), fill = evaluation)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast error by model (lower is better)",
    x = "RMSE (injury reports per week)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- Seasonal naive has the lowest error on the 2025 season and in cross-validation.
- This surprised us: it beat our predicted winners.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. Seasonal naive RMSE is about 19 on 2025 vs. 21 for ETS. Explain why:
once the Week 1 drop is captured, most of what is left is noise, and the complex models
are pulled up by the high 2016 season.
:::

## Forecast for the 2026 season

```{r}
#| label: plot-forecast

fit_full <- weekly_injuries |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(injury_reports ~ lag(17)))

fc_2026 <- fit_full |> forecast(h = 17)

fc_2026 |>
  autoplot(weekly_injuries |> filter(time > 119), level = c(80, 95)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = season_breaks[8:11],
    labels = season_labels[8:11]
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal naive forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Injury reports"
  )
```

- Expect about 80 reports in Week 1, mostly 110–165 per week in Weeks 2–15,
  and up to about 210 in Weeks 16–17.
- The 95% intervals are wide: about ±44 reports per week.
- Seasonal naive repeats 2025, including its unusually high final weeks.

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. Refit on all ten seasons. Read the forecast in plain language: what
a typical week will look like, and how uncertain that is. Check the numbers on this
slide against the plot after rendering.
:::

## Takeaways and limitations

- Weekly injury reports have been flat since 2017; there is no evidence of a rise or fall.
- The season shape (a quiet Week 1, then a plateau) is predictable; week-to-week swings are not.
- For planning, last season's weekly counts are as good a guide as any model we tried.
- Main limitation: counts are reports, not distinct injuries, and the forecasts
  are uncertain (wide intervals).

::: notes
Speaker: [name]. End on the answer to the question for the decision-maker. Leave time for

:::
